item.title: Myths About Infidelity
item.description:
Infidelity

Myths About Infidelity

Much of what people think they know about infidelity is simply not accurate.

Posted June 14, 2026

Key points
  • Infidelity is extremely common, no matter how you define it.
  • There are many common myths about infidelity, which make dealing with it more complicated.
  • People cheat for many reasons; sex is only one, and often not the most important one.

As long as there have been committed couples, there has been infidelity. Broken vows of sexual exclusivity is a recurring theme in Greek tragedy, the Bible, medieval literature, Shakespeare, and the modern tales of Alfred Hitchcock, Frank Sinatra, and Taylor Swift.

Survey data regarding cheating keeps changing as social definitions of cheating evolve. And the invention of cars, telephones, and the internet—not to mention mixed-gender schools and workplaces—have multiplied people’s opportunities for a broader range of physical and emotional relationships.

Infidelity is one of the top reasons people see a therapist, either alone or with a partner. Most people think they know something about infidelity as a general subject, but when it actually occurs in someone’s life, they need to shed any common myths about it quickly.

Here are challenges to some common myths about infidelity.

MYTH: A vigilant partner can prevent infidelity

Is your mate going to cheat? It’s less likely if the relationship is enjoyable, your mate is healthy, the two of you can talk about everything, and the sex is satisfying.

There’s no guarantee. But some partners try to create one. They examine their mate’s mobile phone: records of texting, geo-locaters, email, and actual phone calls. What Sherlock Holmes wouldn’t give for that source of clues! Or they tell their partner “no one-on-one dinners with anyone of the other sex.” Or they demand to check in on a partner at will. When all else fails, they hire a private detective.

It doesn’t work. If your mate is going to cheat, they’re going to cheat. And even if you could prevent infidelity with the right amount of surveillance, is that how you want to live?

MYTH: Infidelity is always about sex

While different, better, or more sex may be the reason for much infidelity, people cheat for other reasons, too. These include anger; a need to prove that they’re attractive or youthful; the need for affection or touching; the need to feel loved; and the need to prove their autonomy.

There’s also a situational dynamic for some people: “I wasn’t looking for it, but when it fell in my lap, I just couldn’t say no.”

When a spouse discovers they’ve been betrayed, they often imagine that it’s been for someone who is younger, sexier, or more attractive in one way or another. They are then surprised when “the other woman” or “other man” isn’t. What betraying spouses often tell me is that the central benefit of the affair was feeling listened to, or important, or sane—not any amazing sex.

MYTH: Some people are just "sex addicts"

Some people who cheat over and over are responding to a diagnosable mental health problem. They may be medicating their depression, or managing their anxiety, or expressing bipolar disorder or OCD. Cheating may be the way a person with borderline personality disorder navigates stressful life situations.

I’m very sympathetic for people who have so much trouble dealing with their emotions. Therapy is usually helpful, and for many, medication has added benefits.

But “addiction” is a state in which a person’s body has seized control of their decision-making. Heroin and nicotine are good examples. When people describe themselves or their mate as a “sex addict,” they usually mean “someone who keeps making sexual decisions whose consequences they don’t like.”

Why do people do that? Typically because they don’t want to face life without the deception, self-indulgence, and denial that would stop protecting them from realities they don’t want to face.

Repetitive promise-breaking may look like addiction, but it’s typically a desperate attempt to avoid the consequences of keeping promises—whether they involve boredom, rage, hopelessness, despair about aging, or a sexless relationship.

By the way, let's notice that the psychology field doesn't have many helpful things to say to people who are trapped in sexless marriages—especially if the partners love each other or if the couple has young children.

MYTH: It’s always better to admit an affair

It depends on what someone is trying to accomplish. If someone’s goal is simply to rid themselves of guilt after an affair ends without discovery, that would be pretty selfish.

Of course, if an affair is discovered by the betrayed partner, it’s generally better to acknowledge it; the additional lying and coverup can easily make things messier, more complicated, and it usually fails. The betrayed partner can also use the additional coverup as evidence that the cheater can’t be trusted in the future, which makes eventual reconciliation almost impossible.

Opening the subject of having, ending, or considering an affair can be a powerful way to start a conversation about wanting to improve a relationship. It certainly will get a partner’s attention.

MYTH: Once a cheater, always a cheater

Surveys estimate that someone who has cheated before is three times more likely to cheat again, compared to those who have never cheated.

On the other hand, my clinical experience is that many cheaters are themselves devastated by the outcome of the affair’s discovery. Whether because of their partner’s grief, their own sense of shame, or both, some cheaters are shocked into fidelity.

Well, first they’re shocked. Then they have to go through a process—therapy, or a spiritual awakening, or a dark night of the soul. If they emerge with a new understanding of themselves, or of intimacy, or of betrayal, they’re then in a position to commit to fidelity. Some of the best marriages are (eventually) built that way.

But while it’s true that some people cheat again and again, it’s inaccurate to say that every cheater does so. And it would be a shame to assume that a one-time cheater is, by definition, a hopeless case.

MYTH: Marriage can’t survive infidelity

If that were true, marriage would be a poor gamble. And marriage counseling would be a poor investment.

There are two kinds of relationships that survive infidelity. In the first, communication is poor; expectations are low; there’s family or cultural pressure to stay together; there may be financial or other dependence. This is a relationship that wasn’t very satisfying before the infidelity. The couple may not work to improve it or to understand each other even after the disruption of infidelity.

The second kind of relationship that survives infidelity is almost the opposite of the first. In it, people work hard to understand what happened, and why. They are introspective to at least some degree. At some point they start listening to each other. And they eventually talk about what they want in the new couple they’re in the process of creating.

Working with those people is a lot of work, but it can also be thrilling and life-affirming, too.

item.title: What Grief Teaches Us About Showing Up
item.description:
Grief

What Grief Teaches Us About Showing Up

When someone is grieving, remembering is support.

Posted June 14, 2026

This week marks two dates I never expected to sit side by side.

My father's birthday was last week. He died suddenly the day after his birthday, a few years ago.

As those dates approach each year, I find myself paying attention not only to my own grief but also to my mother's. The days surrounding these anniversaries carry a particular weight. There is gratitude for the years we had with him, sadness for the years we have missed, and an awareness that life continues to move forward even when part of us remains connected to someone who is gone.

One of the unexpected lessons grief has taught me is that showing up for someone who is grieving is often far less complicated than we imagine.

Many people hesitate to mention a deceased loved one. They worry they might remind the person of their loss or make them sad. The assumption seems to be that grief only surfaces when it is mentioned. But anyone who has lost someone significant knows this isn't how grief works.

The people we love are not forgotten between conversations. They are present in ordinary moments: a smell, a song, a family recipe, an empty chair. Grieving people are already remembering.

Being reminded is not what hurts. What hurts is feeling as though everyone else has forgotten.

Our understanding of bereavement has shifted from the idea that we should "move on" from those we have lost to the idea that maintaining connection with a deceased loved one is common and helpful. The relationship does not end; it changes. We carry the person's influence, values, stories, and memories forward into our lives.

Perhaps this is why simple acts of remembrance can feel so meaningful: A text on a birthday. A note on the anniversary of a death. A shared memory that begins with, "I was thinking about your dad today." These gestures do not intensify grief but ease the loneliness that can accompany it.

Grief is love's continuation. I experience that continuation in small ways. In the moments when I offer guidance to a friend, extend compassion to someone who is struggling, or pause to consider what truly matters, I often recognize traces of my father. His life continues to shape mine, even in his absence.

And one of the most compassionate ways we can show up for those who are grieving is being willing to remember alongside them.

Sometimes the most healing message we can send is simply, "I remembered today too."

item.title: Men Still Wait Too Long to Ask for Help
item.description:
Suicide

Men Still Wait Too Long to Ask for Help

Delay can turn a treatable mental health problem into a crisis.

Posted June 14, 2026

Key points
  • Men wait an average of 11 years after symptoms begin before seeking help for a mental health concern.
  • In the US in 2024 the male suicide rate was nearly four times that of females.
  • Silence often leads to poor sleep, irritability, anger, and risk-taking behaviors.
  • Asking for help can start treatment, ease life pressures, and change the direction of a life story.
Source: Nathan Cowley/ Pexels

Men’s Health Month gives an important reminder: Many men still wait too long to ask for help.

A Depression and Bipolar Support Alliance summary found people wait an average of 11 years after symptoms begin before seeking help for a mental health concern. The CDC reports that suicide was responsible for 48,824 deaths in 2024, and that the suicide rate was nearly four times higher in males than in females. The American Foundation for Suicide Prevention found the same pattern in its 2024 data, reporting that suicide-related deaths were four times higher among males than females.

For many men, the problem is that they hide when something is not right.

Men are taught early to keep going and handle things on their own. They hold onto beliefs that men should “tough it out," but that blocks help. Showing vulnerability can feel like weakness to men raised with these beliefs. Some tell themselves that the system will not understand them. Some believe that reaching out will make them a burden to others. Those thoughts keep them from asking for support.

From the outside, these responses can feel like strength, but these delays carry real costs: Sleep gets worse. Routine work gets harder. Fatigue limits what a person can do. Stress shows up as anger, alcohol or drug use, risk-taking, irritability, or withdrawal. Many men push through pain until they can’t ignore it anymore. Silence builds for years, then turns into a crisis that feels sudden. Sometimes it builds to the point of suicide.

This is why Men’s Health Month matters.

It gives us a chance to normalize mental health conversations. The conversation begins with awareness, but it also has to move from the silent struggle to action. Saying “I am not okay” is often the hardest step, but it is an essential first step. That act can change the direction of the story and provide a path for treatment to begin.

That ripple effect matters; one brave decision can shift more than one life.

Men’s Health Month is a time to say this plainly: Asking for help is not weakness. For many men, it can be the first real step toward getting well.

If you or someone you love is contemplating suicide, seek help immediately. For help 24/7 dial 988 for the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, or reach out to the Crisis Text Line by texting TALK to 741741. To find a therapist near you, visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.

item.title: Eleonore Frankl, 1925–2026: An Obituary
item.description:
Psychology

Eleonore Frankl, 1925–2026: An Obituary

Eleonore Frankl helped sustain Viktor Frankl’s postwar life and work.

Posted June 14, 2026

Key points
  • Eleonore Frankl helped sustain Viktor Frankl’s postwar life and work.
  • Her warmth made Frankl’s message of meaning more human and accessible.
  • She saw people as persons, not as titles, achievements, or public roles.
  • Her life shows that great intellectual work is often sheltered by love.

With the passing of Eleonore Frankl, née Schwindt, known to so many simply and affectionately as Elly, a life has come to its quiet close that cannot be measured merely by the years between November 6, 1925, and June 10, 2026. For one hundred years she lived in Vienna and from Vienna; yet her presence reached far beyond the city of her birth — not least because, together with her husband, Viktor Frankl, she circled the globe many times in the service of his pioneering work: the Third Viennese School of Psychotherapy, known by the double name of Logotherapy and Existential Analysis.

Born Eleonore Katharina Schwindt, she came from modest circumstances in Kaisermühlen, a district of Vienna marked not by grandeur but by closeness to ordinary life (1). The hardships of her youth did not make her hard. On the contrary, they seem to have given her that practical intelligence and direct humanity which so many later remembered in her: a woman without affectation, without false solemnity, without any taste for theatrical importance — but above all with humour, quickness, vitality, and an open heart.

During the Second World War, she worked as a nurse in the dental department of the Vienna Policlinic. It was there, in the immediate aftermath of the Holocaust, that she met Viktor E. Frankl, who had returned to Vienna after the concentration camps. Much has been written about Frankl’s survival, his thought, and his extraordinary intellectual achievement. Less can ever be adequately said about what it means for a person, after such losses, to be met again by life — not as hope in the abstract, but in the living form of another human being.

In a letter to a fellow survivor from the Dachau camp complex in March 1946, Frankl wrote of his despair and loneliness: relatives, friends, colleagues — most of them either murdered in the Holocaust or scattered into distant exile. But only weeks later, on May 19, 1946, Frankl had something else to report (2): “What I wrote to you in my last letter — everything has changed. One human being has changed everything.” Elly Frankl.

They married in 1947, and their daughter Gabriele was born the same year. For the next 50 years, until Viktor Frankl’s death in 1997, Elly was his wife, companion, helper, witness, and home. To call her simply “the wife of Viktor Frankl” is both true and far too little. She did not merely accompany a famous man. She helped make possible the human conditions under which his work could continue, mature, and travel into the world. In the books, lectures, journeys, meetings, correspondence, visitors, obligations, and countless daily demands, there was Elly as much as Viktor Frankl.

Jacob Needleman (1) once described her beautifully as “the warmth that accompanies the light.” Viktor Frankl’s work brought light to the lives of millions — people trapped in grief, displacement, everyday suffering, or in the experience of a life felt to be meaningless; people caught in routine, indifference, dependency, depression, aggression, or cynicism. What Needleman meant, perhaps, was that in her own unique way, Elly helped make that light inhabitable.

I had the great good fortune, between 1999 and 2007, to see Elly Frankl often and, soon enough, to be honoured by her friendship. During those years I worked in the private estate of Viktor Frankl — the Viktor Frankl Archive in Vienna — in the Frankl apartment, as it was known throughout the city. In those years I sometimes visited Elly weekly, sometimes even more often. Each time she had set out biscuits, coffee, and juices. Officially, I was supposed to be working in the archive; in truth, however, we often spent hours in conversation — and in laughter. Laughter mattered greatly to her.

Later I was able to come less frequently, as I started a family of my own. Yet even here Elly played her part: It was in that very apartment that I fell in love with the woman who has now been my wife for almost twenty years. My wife is a photographer, and at the time we were working together on an illustrated volume on Viktor Frankl’s Vienna (3). It was through this work that it happened: we fell in love. Yet Elly saw it before either of us had quite admitted it. One day, during one of the photo sessions in the Frankl apartment, she watched us closely; then, after Juliane had gone out to buy fresh rolls of film, Elly looked at me with that rare mixture of maternal warmth and mischievous amusement and said: “I think you and Juliane have found more than just a book project together.”

She was right.

These are only a few glimpses of how I experienced Elly, as so many others did before and after me—as a person of disarming immediacy. She could laugh. She could speak plainly. She could be moved. She could remember. She could also, with the freedom of someone who had no need to impress, cut through exaggeration or sentimentality.

She had known Eleanor Roosevelt, Martin Heidegger, Sophie Freud, Abraham Maslow, Karl Jaspers, Pope Paul VI, the Gorbachevs, Konrad Lorenz, Hillary Clinton — all of them, and many more (1). But when she spoke of such people, she did not speak primarily of what they did. She received and perceived people not as representatives of institutions, but as persons. And one question mattered to her when she described them: whether they had remained ordinary, approachable human beings — and whether they could laugh. That was how she saw people. And this is perhaps why so many who met her felt that they had encountered not only the widow of a great thinker, but someone who herself had understood, in the most immediate way, what it means to remain true to oneself.

After Viktor Frankl’s death, for nearly three further decades, she preserved memories, opened doors, corrected misunderstandings, welcomed scholars and students, and remained connected with the international community of logotherapy. Even in very old age, stories were told of her listening patiently to people who came with questions, distress, admiration, or need.

Her contribution was publicly recognized through honorary doctorates, including one from North Park University in Chicago and another from the Moscow Institute of Psychoanalysis. Yet such honours, deserved as they were, only partially capture her significance.

Elly Frankl also represented a bridge—between generations, between Judaism and Christianity, between memory and future, between scholarship and ordinary kindness. A Catholic woman married to a Jewish survivor and thinker, she lived a marriage marked by deep respect for the sacred background of the other. In that quiet mutual reverence there was a lesson perhaps as important as many formal doctrines: that love need not erase difference in order to honour it. It may, instead, create a home in which difference is neither denied nor dramatized, but held in tenderness.

Great works do not arise from intellect alone. They are often sheltered by love.

I remember her with gratitude as a woman of warmth, strength, independence, humour, and fidelity. We honour her not only because she stood beside Viktor Frankl, but because she stood so fully, so vividly, and so lovingly as herself.

May her memory remain a blessing.

item.title: Father's Day and the Grief Nobody Talks About
item.description:
Grief

Father's Day and the Grief Nobody Talks About

Not every Father's Day is a celebration. Some are just getting through it.

Posted June 14, 2026

Key points
  • Grieving a parent who is still alive is real grief, even if nobody around you treats it that way.
  • You can love your father and still dread Father's Day. Both things can be true at the same time.
  • Estranged adult children are often told to fix it when what they need is acknowledgment of the loss.

Every year, Father's Day arrives right on schedule. For some people, so does everything they've been trying not to think about or feel. The posts, the tributes, the throwback photos, the messages about how Dad was always there sometimes start appearing the week before. For a lot of people, that reflects something real and worth celebrating. For others, it is a reminder of something that was never there, or something that was there and then wasn't, or something so complicated there are sometimes not words to describe it.

Not everyone has a father to call. And for those who do, not everyone wants to or are able to. Some people lost their dad to death, some lost him to addiction, mental illness, a significant other, or years of silence that eventually became permanent. And some never had a father in the picture at all. Others had one who showed up physically but was never quite there in the ways that mattered. And then there are people dealing with something that gets talked about far less—grieving a father who is still alive.

That last one is its own particular kind of hard. When a parent dies, there is grief of course, but there is also structure around it. There is a funeral, there are people who acknowledge your loss and support you, there is a cultural script for what comes next. When a parent is still alive but the relationship is gone, or never really existed, none of that is there. You know where he is and you could theoretically call. But you do not, or he does not, or he doesn’t answer if you do, and the door that should feel open stays closed. There is no ceremony for that. Most people will not even recognize it as loss. And people might still ask about him and bring him up to you often.

Source: Rachel Needle

Understanding Ambiguous Loss and Estrangement

Pauline Boss, a family therapist who has spent decades studying this phenomenon, called it ambiguous loss. The term originally described situations like a missing person, but the concept extends to relationships where someone is psychologically absent even when they are physically reachable, or psychologically present even when they are gone (Boss, 2006). Estrangement tends to fall into this category, and so does the long, quiet grief of a relationship that never became what you needed it to be, or one that did and no longer is. What makes it especially complicated is that for some, hope tends to stay alive. The person is still there, so things could, theoretically, change. Research on estrangement finds that adult children often remain caught between the desire to make meaning of what happened and the ongoing uncertainty about whether the relationship could ever be repaired (Scharp & Thomas, 2016). That possibility can be a comfort, but it can also keep you stuck or even frozen, cycling between hoping, being disappointed, and bracing for the next round of it. It is exhausting in a way that is genuinely hard to explain to people who have not lived it.

The social piece adds another layer. Estranged adult children frequently feel isolated or stigmatized, often encountering pressure from friends and family to reconcile rather than receiving any real acknowledgment of their loss (Scharp & Thomas, 2016) or understanding of why the distance exists. This is especially difficult when it is not the adult child’s choice to be distanced. On a holiday when everyone around you seems to be celebrating, that silence can feel especially loud. The message, spoken or not, is often some version of: you should fix this. What people in that position usually need instead is for someone to recognize that what they are carrying and feeling is real.

And underneath all of this, there is often love, which is the part that surprises people sometimes. You can love someone and still feel deeply hurt by them. You can miss a father who was not good to you or was and no longer is. You can feel grateful for certain things while grieving the things that were or currently are missing. These are not contradictions but rather they are just what it looks like to love a person who is complicated or has changed, which is most people.

Coping Strategies for Those Who Struggle on Father’s Day

If Father's Day is hard for you, one of the most useful things you can do is stop trying to make yourself feel differently than you do. Not every holiday has to be an opportunity for resolution or reflection or gratitude. Sometimes it is just a hard day, and the kindest thing you can do for yourself is move through it without piling expectation on top of pain that is already there.

For those fortunate enough to have a loving relationship with their father, celebrate it genuinely. Post the photo, make the call, have the brunch. None of that needs to stop or change. But it is worth acknowledging and holding some awareness that the people around you may be having a completely different experience of the exact same day. You do not have to say anything about it and you do not have to change what you are doing. Just knowing it tends to make people a little more empathic, or a little more gentle, in how they interact with and show up to others. Compassion does not ask you to minimize your own joy; it just asks you to remember that your experience is not everyone's.

What's hard about a holiday like this is that the people around you are all having completely different experiences of the same day, and most of them are not talking about it. The person smiling at brunch might be holding something heavy. You probably can't tell. That's worth remembering, whether yours is something to celebrate or something to survive.

item.title: How to Deal With Your Emotionally Neglectful Parents
item.description:
Self-Help

How to Deal With Your Emotionally Neglectful Parents

Understanding your parents matters, but protecting yourself matters more.

Posted June 14, 2026

Key points
  • Healing from emotional neglect doesn't require involving one's parents in the process.
  • The type of parent one has determines if discussing neglect will help or hinder healing.
  • Having compassion for emotionally neglectful parents can ease pain, but should not replace self-protection.
Source: InsideCreativeHouse/StockAdobe

Now that I see what my parents didn’t give me, how do I continue to interact with them?

Should I tell my parents how they failed me?

If I talk to my parents about childhood emotional neglect, won’t it make them feel bad?

How do I handle the pain that I feel now, as an adult, each time my parents treat my feelings like they don’t matter?

If you were raised by parents who were not tuned in enough to your emotional needs, you have probably experienced the effects of this failure over and over in your adult life. Once you realize how deeply you have been affected by childhood emotional neglect, it can become quite difficult to interact with the parents who neglected you.

One of the most frequent questions that I am asked by people who grew up with childhood emotional neglect is, “Should I talk to my parents about it?”

This is not an easy question to answer because no two childhoods are the same. In fact, the number of possible answers is as infinite as the many ways that childhood emotional neglect can happen. It can be healing when an adult child and parent come to a mutual understanding of how an emotional failure happened and why, and how it affected everyone involved. This, however, can be a complicated business, difficult, and even risky.

It’s important to keep in mind that you don’t have to include your parents in your recovery. As an adult, you can identify what you didn’t get and begin giving it to yourself. Many people do this successfully without ever including their parents.

That said, you may feel a wish or need to reach some understanding with them. If so, one extremely important factor to consider is the type of emotionally neglectful parents that you have.

The 3 Main Categories of Emotionally Neglectful Parents

  1. Self-centered, Abusive, or Multiple-Failure Parents: These parents expect their child to fulfill their needs, rather than the other way around. They may not have treated you with the physical and emotional care and protection that a child needs from a parent.
  2. Struggling: These parents may mean well, but they are struggling in their own lives. They may be struggling financially, emotionally, or with the caretaking of a sick family member or child.
  3. WMBNT or Well-Meaning-But-Neglected-Themselves: These parents love their children and give them everything they can. But they are not able to give their child enough emotional responsiveness and validation because they didn’t receive it in their own childhoods. They may be simply “emotion blind.”

Parents who are in the last two categories stand a better chance of getting past their initial hurt, guilt, or defensiveness to have a productive conversation. If your parents fall into the self-centered or abusive category, see the section called “Self-centered, Abusive, or Multiple-failure Parents” below.

5 Ways to Talk With Your Emotionally Neglectful Parents

  1. Ask about their childhoods. Learning about your parents’ upbringing may help you understand how their emotional blind spots developed. This understanding can reduce the sting of their behavior, whether or not you talk with them.
  2. Try to find compassion. Often, seeing how your parents were affected by their own upbringing can soften anger and frustration.
  3. Anticipate and prepare. Think about how each parent might respond to the topic of childhood emotional neglect. Will they feel guilty, confused, defensive, or angry? Is one more open than the other?
  4. If possible, take a chance. If you feel there is a potential for positive results and healing, I suggest that you take a chance and talk about it.
  5. Talk with compassion and awareness. Choose a calm moment. Speak in person if possible. Frame this as a discovery about yourself, not an accusation. Explain how invisible and easy it is for emotional neglect to happen, even in loving families. Share what you are doing to heal, and emphasize that your goal is to move forward and feel closer.

Self-centered, Abusive, or Multiple Failure Parents

If you have parents who fall into one of these categories, the situation is more complex. Unless they have changed, they may not be able to understand emotional neglect or respond in a healthy way.

For you, there is one guiding principle. Make your decision based solely upon your own needs. If you think it may strengthen you or help you, even if it creates distance, then do it. If not, then do not. You are not obligated to take your parents’ needs and preferences into account. On this, it’s all about you.

Parents who were abusive to you as a child, either verbally, emotionally, physically, or sexually, are also, by definition, emotionally neglectful. If they had been emotionally attuned to you enough, they would not have been able to treat you this way.

If your parents were/are abusive in any way, then it may be of more value to talk with them about the abuse than about the neglect, since abuse is far more visible and tangible than childhood emotional neglect. Because childhood emotional neglect can be so imperceptible and hides beneath abuse, it will be very difficult and unlikely for abusive parents to ever grasp the concept.

Unless your parents have done meaningful work to change, they may not be able to hear you now any more than they could when you were a child.

So, ask yourself, “What is likely to happen if you bring this up?” Will they dismiss you, become angry, or turn it against you?“

If so, your energy may be better spent focusing on your own healing.

If you do decide to talk with them, you must be prepared to protect yourself emotionally. You will need enough strength not to be harmed by their reaction. This is not easy, especially when you were raised this way.

The Takeaway

You do not need to talk to your parents to heal from childhood emotional neglect. You can do this work on your own. Understanding your parents and developing compassion for them may help ease your pain. In some cases, sharing this understanding can improve your relationship.

But this decision is deeply personal. It depends on who your parents are and what you need. There is no single right answer. Only the one that supports your healing.

The original version of this post appears on emotionalneglect.com.

item.title: Evolutionary Mismatch and Spiritual Degradation
item.description:
Evolutionary Psychology

Evolutionary Mismatch and Spiritual Degradation

What scholars agree on about technology and the threat to human flourishing.

Posted June 14, 2026

Key points
  • Religious and atheist scholars agree: Modern life is mismatched with human nature.
  • Smartphones and urban anonymity are driving anxiety, loneliness, and declining trust.
  • Digital substitutes are weakening real relationships and intimacy across generations.
  • Restoring community, sacredness, and attention are key to human flourishing.
Source: Gemini AI image/Free use

One of the virtues of a post-tribal outlook is that nearly everyone becomes a potential conversation partner. Rather than seeking opportunities to tout or distinguish one’s own views, the impulse is to find common ground with others, whatever their political, religious, or ideological commitments.

An encouraging (though troubling) example is the growing convergence between some religious and atheist scholars on the dangers of evolutionary mismatch—that is, the ways modern environments and technologies are increasingly out of step with human nature and human flourishing.

What Religious and Atheist Scholars Both Say About Modern Life

In Thriving With Stone Age Minds, Christian psychologists Justin L. Barrett and Pamela Ebstyne King examine human behavior through a lens not typically associated with theological scholarship: evolutionary psychology. They argue that our “Stone Age minds” come equipped with deep social needs that are increasingly mismatched with modern life. Their thesis resonates with arguments advanced by social psychologist Jonathan Haidt in The Anxious Generation and neuroscientist Debra Soh in Sextinction.

Evolutionary psychologists begin their examinations of human behavior by considering the environments in which humans spent most of their history: small communities of 150 or fewer people where nearly everyone knew one another. Life unfolded through repeated interactions, shared norms, and reciprocal obligations. These conditions shaped a psychology oriented toward face-to-face relationships, trust, and a balance between self-interest and communal responsibility.

Modern life differs dramatically. In large urban settings, people encounter countless strangers with whom they have no ongoing relationship or social obligation. At the same time, advertising and digital technologies constantly encourage immediate gratification. Barrett and King argue that these conditions weaken social bonds and erode empathy and trust—a view supported by the broad decline in institutional trust across government, media, higher education, and the courts in recent decades.

The Consequences of Living Online

The most consequential mismatch may involve smartphones and social media. Though the phrase may sound trite or alarmist—“it’s the phones!”—the evidence reviewed by Haidt suggests that the migration of childhood and adolescence online has coincided with a dramatic deterioration in youth mental health.

Among the troubling trends Haidt highlights:

  • Unstructured time with friends has declined sharply, while loneliness has increased.
  • Anxiety and depression have risen substantially among younger generations since 2010.
  • Suicide rates have increased dramatically among both girls and boys.

For Haidt, the replacement of a play-based childhood with a phone-based childhood is the major culprit. Ubiquitous screens clash with the natural developmental process of childhood free play and appear to be rewiring young brains in harmful ways. Synchronous group play—where children must navigate complex human relationships in real time—is likely how childhood unfolded for most of human evolutionary history. Replacing it with screen-based experiences has deprived young people of essential developmental experiences linked to risky play and autonomous, organic relationships.

Source: DeepAI image/Free use

The news regarding intimacy is equally troubling. Soh echoes Haidt’s concern that living online harms social development, particularly among younger generations. She notes that Gen Z spends an average of 6.5 hours per day on their phones, with Millennials and Gen X not far behind.

Among the trends she highlights:

  • Sexual inactivity among young men has more than doubled since the early 2000s.
  • Rates of sexlessness have risen among Millennials.
  • Fifty-seven percent of single American adults report that they are not actively seeking a romantic relationship.

As Soh argues, modern technologies provide endless digital substitutes for intimacy while reducing opportunities to develop the social skills required for real-world relationships. Pornography, dating apps, social media, and other forms of digital stimulation can satisfy immediate desires while discouraging the effort, vulnerability, and persistence required to build lasting relationships. In this context, it is striking that 45 percent of men aged 18 to 25 report never having approached a woman in person for a date.

We are, in effect, running a vast social experiment. Anonymous urban living, hyper-individualism, and diverse forms of digital distraction and stimulation have created environments profoundly different from those in which human psychology evolved.

Reducing Screen Time Is Not Enough

Solutions require more than simply reducing screen time. The deeper challenge is cultivating environments that foster the relationships, virtues, and sources of meaning humans need to flourish. Here, Haidt’s emphasis on restoring practices of sacredness, embodiment, attention, and community overlaps significantly with Barrett and King’s vision of human thriving and divine purpose.

In language unusual for an atheist scholar, Haidt warns of “spiritual degradation” unless societies actively create spaces and times for communal activity, stillness, awe, and elevated moral purpose. For Barrett and King, the same modern conditions pull people away from their God-given telos. Despite profoundly different metaphysical foundations, both perspectives agree that many pressing social problems stem from the mismatch between human nature and the world we have built.

In an age of deep ideological and metaphysical disagreement, we should not fetishize our differences. Religious and nonreligious observers increasingly recognize that contemporary culture is undermining the relationships, habits, and institutions essential to human flourishing. Acknowledging this shared concern is a vital first step toward repairing it.

item.title: Catching Sight: Letting Guide Dogs Lead the Way as Teammates
item.description:
Relationships

Catching Sight: Letting Guide Dogs Lead the Way as Teammates

Deni Elliott explains the transformative power of human-animal relationships.

Posted June 14, 2026

Key points
  • "Catching Sight" shares a woman’s journey through progressive blindness with her extraordinary guide dog.
  • Deni Elliott's book is full of her correcting mistakes and becoming aware of her authentic self.
  • There are thousands of guide dogs globally with different temperaments matched perfectly with their humans.
Source: Gustavo Fring/Pexels

Many people rely on assistance dogs for support, and the well-being of all participants in these interactions is essential and must be given careful attention. To be sure that the dogs' and their humans' physical and emotional well-being receive the focus they require can take time and patience and isn't always easy to achieve. For this and other reasons, I was thrilled to learn about a new book titled Catching Sight: How a Guide Dog Helped Me See Myself by Deni Elliott with Graham Buck that brings readers into the incredible world of guide dogs to show why these close partnerships matter—not just for mobility, but for dignity and belonging.

Deni Elliott’s powerful story and journey through progressive blindness and the extraordinary guide dog who kept her safe will stay with you long after you finish reading this transformative book. When ethics scholar Deni realized she could no longer navigate the world safely alone, she turned to a guide dog—a decision that reshaped her understanding of disability and independence. Catching Sight offers a behind-the-scenes look at the world of guide dog breeding and training, revealing the intelligence and decision-making skills these dogs develop from birth.

Marc Bekoff: Why did you write Catching Sight?

Deni Elliott: I want to share with readers what I learned about dogs and myself when I learned how to partner with a professionally trained guide dog. When I met the little yellow Labrador retriever, Alberta, at Guiding Eyes for the Blind, I was blown away by the difference between Alberta and my two previous privately trained guide dogs. The privately trained dogs were task-trained, with the help of a service dog training professional, to lead me around obstacles and elevation changes that I could not see.

Guide dog school puppies are different from task-trained dogs. From birth, each puppy is celebrated for being confident and for thinking critically and creatively. The goal is that at the end of advanced training, when the dog is approximately 2 years old, the dog understands that they are expected to keep their human partner safe when the two are linked through the guide dog harness. If the dog has demonstrated to the trainers that they want this kind of life, only then will they be matched with a visually disabled human partner.

The dog has learned to use their superior senses of smell and hearing in addition to their vision to guide their person; they have learned how to communicate with people. In guide dog school, the human client learns to understand what the dog is telling them and to communicate clearly to the dog in return. The human client learns to trust the dog over their own instincts.

Source: Beacon Press, used with permission

Despite my previous experience with pet dogs and dogs who I trained to compete in obedience, agility, and rally, it was new to me to respect my dog as a collaborator who had a broad understanding of our shared work. Through my Guiding Eyes instructor, Graham Buck, who worked with me on Catching Sight, I learned it was safe to trust a dog with my life.

MB: How does your book relate to your background and general areas of interest?

DE: I grew up near Washington, D.C., and was active in civil rights, women's rights, and disability rights. I believed that the activism and advocacy of the 1960s and '70s made the world a better place. I wanted a career in which I could help others feel powerful enough to make the world a better place.

I wrote extensively while teaching ethics in undergraduate, graduate, and professional education. I think that Catching Sight illustrates one of the ways that people can form and maintain ethical relationships with dogs. It shows how people and dogs both benefit from canine-human relationships based on true interdependence. My guide dog and I collaborate and communicate to work together, yet our dependence upon each other is entirely different from the other.

While writing Catching Sight, I realized how hard it had been for me to accept my own limitations. The book is full of me making mistakes, working to correct those mistakes, and becoming more aware of my authentic self in the process. Humans are fallible and vulnerable. I taught that as an ethics professor; Catching Sight reveals how I lived that reality.

MB: Who do you hope to reach?

DE: I hope to reach people who pass a guide dog team out on the street and wonder, "What is going on there?" I hope to reach people who like dogs but who have not been introduced to the canine capacities evident in a professionally bred and trained guide dog. I hope to reach people who have a limited understanding of disability. I hope to introduce readers to cultures in which visual ability can be irrelevant, such as that on the Guiding Eyes for the Blind campus. I wrote in the book that the only staff members I knew to be fully sighted were those driving the van.

MB: What are some of the topics you consider and what are some of your major messages?

DE: The amazing array of canine capacities is the major topic. Dogs can take on responsibilities in canine-human relationships. Dogs want to share their canine-based perceptions with their people. My major message for readers is to respond to canine capacities by basing relationships with dogs on affirmation and positivity, just as we should strive to do in our human-to-human interpersonal relationships.

MB: How does your work differ from others that are concerned with some of the same general topics?

DE: Catching Sight includes material collected through dozens of interviews. I wanted to tell how dogs learn to make the necessary choices for them to be safely matched with visually impaired human partners. I wanted to include the point of view of my veteran Guiding Eyes trainer, Graham Buck, as a balance to my first-time-in-guide-dog-school perspective. Catching Sight is unique in combining the client's voice with that of the volunteers and professionals who make guide dogs possible.

Alberta evaluates Deni's swing.
Source: Deni Elliott, used with permission

MB: Are you hopeful that as people learn more about your experiences, it will change how they view you and your extraordinary guide dog?

DE: I hope readers will see me as a person who learned from some of her mistakes; I hope they see Alberta as a guide dog well-suited for partnership with me. I hope they realize that there are thousands of working guide dogs around the world with different temperaments who are matched perfectly with their human partners. I hope that readers can take something from Catching Sight that will help them be more accepting of human limitations and more appreciative of canine abilities.
